Last month, I was impacted by a company-wide layoff. 

Taking a month to step back, process everything, and reset gave me some unexpected perspective. Here are 4 things I learned:

1. Your job is what you do, not who you are.
When your Slack and email get cut off in an instant, you realize how much identity you tied to a company badge. Detangling self-worth from employment was the hardest, but most necessary, shift.

2. People remember how you treated them.
The outpouring of messages, intros, and kind check-ins from former colleagues, clients, and managers was overwhelming. Relationships are truly the only long-term currency in your career.

3. Resilience is a muscle you build in real-time.
The first week was shock. The second was anxiety. But by week three, it turned into clarity about what I actually want next—and what I don't.

4. A forced pause is often an overlooked gift.
In the day-to-day grind, we rarely ask ourselves: "Am I still moving in the direction I want?" This detour gave me the space to answer that honestly.

To anyone else navigating a transition right now: be kind to yourself. It’s a chapter, not the whole book.

I’m now actively exploring new opportunities in [Your Domain/Role]. If you know of any open roles or just want to connect, I’d love to chat!

Most companies that struggle with remote work don’t actually have a remote work problem.

They have a trust problem and a documentation problem.

During the pandemic, a lot of teams took their in-office habits and copied them directly into Slack and Zoom:
- 8 hours of back-to-back video calls
- Expecting instant replies on Slack all day
- Tracking mouse movements or status dots
- Still relying on informal "hallway catchups" to make major decisions

That’s not remote work; that’s just office surveillance in sweatpants. It burns people out and kills deep work.

The companies doing remote work well operate completely differently:
1. They write everything down. Context lives in public docs, not private DMs or someone's head.
2. They default to asynchronous communication. Most updates don’t need a meeting.
3. They measure output and outcomes, not hours spent sitting in front of a webcam.

When you give capable people clear goals, proper documentation, and autonomy, you don't need to micromanage where they sit.

Early in my career, I made a careless mistake that took down a client dashboard for almost an hour.

I remember sitting at my desk, heart pounding, terrified of what my manager would say. When I finally walked into his office to tell him, I was ready to be reprimanded.

He listened quietly, turned to his whiteboard, and asked just two questions:
1. "What do we need to do right now to fix it for the client?"
2. "What guardrails did we fail to give you so this could happen in the first place?"

No anger, no blaming, no public humiliation. We fixed the issue together, updated our deployment pipeline that afternoon, and moved on.

That 15-minute conversation taught me more about leadership than any management book ever has. 

Great managers don't look for someone to blame when things go sideways. They look at the system, protect their people, and turn failures into teaching moments.

It’s been years, but whenever someone on my team makes a mistake today, I try to channel that exact same reaction.

A lot of people think AI is going to replace marketers. 

I don't think that's what's happening. What AI is actually replacing is lazy marketing.

Right now, feeds and inboxes are being flooded with generic, formulaic AI-generated blog posts, copy, and LinkedIn updates. It takes 10 seconds to generate 1,000 words of polished fluff that says absolutely nothing new.

Because the cost of producing generic content has dropped to zero, the value of that content has also dropped to zero.

So where does that leave actual marketers?

The things that will stand out now are the things an LLM can't fake:
- Real, messy point-of-view based on lived experience
- Original research and proprietary data
- True customer empathy and deep taste
- Actual relationships and human storytelling

AI is an incredible assistant for research, drafting, and organizing your thoughts. But if your entire marketing strategy is prompting a bot and hitting publish, you're just adding to the noise.

The future of marketing isn't automated volume; it's distinct point-of-view.

It’s finally live! 📱🚀

5 things I wish someone told me when I started as a junior developer:

1. Asking questions after 30 minutes of being stuck isn't a weakness; it's basic efficiency. Spend 20-30 minutes digging into the docs, testing assumptions, and formulating the problem. If you’re still blocked, ask. Your team would rather answer a 2-minute question than watch you lose 2 days.

2. Reading code matters more than writing it. You’ll spend far more time navigating existing codebases than typing brand-new files. Get comfortable reading PRs, tracing unfamiliar functions, and learning how senior engineers structure solutions.

3. Git is forgiving. Don't be terrified of breaking things. Learn how branching, stashing, and commit history work early on. Almost everything can be undone.

4. Clear variable names beat clever one-liners every single time. Write code for the tired developer who will have to maintain it at 2 AM six months from now (which will probably be you).

5. Imposter syndrome doesn’t magically vanish when you get promoted. Tech moves fast and nobody knows everything. The skill isn't knowing all the answers; it's knowing how to figure things out.

What’s one piece of advice you’d add to this list?

Two years ago, I took the leap and started my first company. 

Last week, we officially shut it down.

Writing this isn't easy. On LinkedIn, we celebrate the funding rounds, the hockey-stick graphs, and the exits. We rarely talk about what it feels like when you pour your savings, your weekends, and your sanity into an idea—and it still doesn't work.

Here is what went wrong:
1. We built for too long before validating whether customers would actually pay for the solution, not just say "that's cool."
2. We tried to serve everyone instead of dominating a narrow, painful niche.
3. We ran out of runway before finding repeatable distribution.

It hurts. I feel responsible to our early believers, customers, and team.

But I don't regret doing it. In the last 24 months, I learned more about product, sales, cash flow, and emotional resilience than in the previous ten years of my career combined. 

Failure is a brutal teacher, but it is an honest one.

Taking a couple of weeks to rest, reflect, and spend time with family. Then, onto the next chapter. 

To everyone who supported us along the way: thank you from the bottom of my heart.

We talk a lot about burnout in tech and corporate life, but we usually talk about it after someone has already crashed.

For a long time, I treated exhaustion like a badge of honor. Late-night emails, working through sick days, skipping lunch to squeeze in one more meeting. I thought that was just "what high performance looked like."

It wasn't. It was just unsustainable.

Eventually, the lack of boundaries caught up with me: brain fog, irritability, zero creativity, and dreading Monday mornings.

Here is what I've learned about mental health at work:
• Rest is not a reward you earn after finishing everything; it's a prerequisite to doing good work.
• If your company culture makes people feel guilty for using their PTO, that's not high performance—that's poor management.
• Setting boundaries (closing your laptop at 6 PM, not having Slack on your personal phone) doesn't make you a bad teammate. It makes you a durable one.

Take care of yourself this week. The work will still be there tomorrow.

A small customer service interaction yesterday reminded me of a fundamental business truth.

I ordered a part for my home office setup from a small hardware company online. When the package arrived, one small mounting bracket was missing.

I sent an email to support expecting the typical runaround: 
- Fill out a 5-step form
- Send photos of the box
- Wait 5–7 business days for a bot response

Instead, within 20 minutes, I got a reply from a real person named Marcus:
"So sorry about that! That’s on us. I just overnighted the missing bracket to your address—tracking number attached. No need to return anything or fill out forms."

The part probably cost them $3 to make and $10 to ship. 

Did they lose money on that transaction? Yes.
Did they just earn a customer who will buy from them for life and recommend them to colleagues? Absolutely.

Great customer experience isn't about complex loyalty programs or fancy automation. It’s about removing friction, taking ownership when things go wrong, and treating customers like human beings.

And that's a wrap on INSEAD! 🎓

Contrarian take: hustle culture isn’t a sign of ambition. Most of the time, it’s just a symptom of poor prioritization.

Bragging about 80-hour workweeks, surviving on 4 hours of sleep, and never taking a vacation isn't the flex people think it is.

If you consistently need 80 hours a week to hit your goals, one of three things is usually true:
1. You don't know how to delegate.
2. You're working on low-leverage tasks that move the needle by 1%.
3. Your business model or management structure is fundamentally broken.

Real high performers don't measure value in sweat and exhaustion. They measure it in leverage and judgment.

One high-quality decision made with a clear, rested mind will always beat 20 frantic hours of busywork.

Work hard, absolutely. But stop glorifying exhaustion.

Last week, my newsletter crossed 10,000 subscribers. 

No viral TikToks, no paid ads, and no overnight growth hacks. It took me 18 months of writing every single Sunday morning.

If you’re trying to build an audience from zero, here are the 4 things that actually moved the needle:

1. Specificity beats broad appeal.
When I started, I wrote about generic "business and productivity." Growth was dead flat. When I narrowed it down to actionable teardowns for early-stage B2B founders, people finally had a reason to subscribe and share it with their co-founders.

2. Consistency is a trust mechanism.
Publishing at the exact same day and time every week told readers I took their inbox seriously. People unsubscribe from inconsistency faster than they do from mediocre content.

3. Borrowing distribution.
For the first 1,000 subscribers, nobody knew who I was. I spent hours leaving thoughtful comments on relevant LinkedIn posts, participating in niche communities, and doing newsletter swaps with writers at my level.

4. Optimizing for replies, not just clicks.
At the end of every issue, I asked a simple question and replied to every single person who wrote back. Those early readers became my biggest evangelists.

Growing an audience is slow, unglamorous work. But compounding is real if you stick around long enough for it to kick in.

Networking advice is almost always written by extroverts, for extroverts.

"Work the room!"
"Talk to at least 20 people!"
"Grab coffee with everyone you meet!"

For introverts, that sounds exhausting, transactional, and deeply unnatural.

If large events drain your energy, here is a playbook that actually works:

1. Aim for depth, not volume.
Your goal shouldn't be collecting 30 business cards. Aim to have 1 or 2 genuinely interesting conversations. A single meaningful connection is worth ten polite, forgotten chats.

2. Arrive early.
Walking into a crowded, loud room of 100 people already in tight conversational circles is overwhelming. Arriving 15 minutes early when there are only 5 people makes it much easier to strike up a low-key 1-on-1 chat.

3. Ask thoughtful questions and just listen.
Introverts are naturally great listeners. You don't have to be charismatic or dominate the floor. Ask open-ended questions: "What project are you most excited about right now?" or "What brought you to this event?" People love talking about their passions.

4. Connect asynchronously on LinkedIn.
You don't need to network in person to build an incredible professional circle. Writing thoughtful comments on people's posts or sending a personalized, zero-ask DM can build relationships on your own terms.

Networking doesn't require being the loudest person in the room. Quiet curiosity works just as well.

I spent five years in B2B sales early in my career, and looking back, it taught me more about human nature and life than any classroom ever did.

A few lessons that stayed with me:

1. "No" rarely means "never."
Most of the time, it just means "not right now" or "I don't understand how this helps me yet." Learning not to take rejection personally in sales completely rewired how I handle setbacks in my personal life.

2. Listening is ten times more persuasive than pitching.
The worst salespeople talk the entire meeting. The best ones ask great questions, shut up, and let the customer explain their world. In relationships, parenting, and leadership, people just want to feel heard before they care what you have to say.

3. Urgency can't be manufactured; it has to be discovered.
You can't force someone to care about a problem they don't believe they have. You have to find where the pain already exists.

4. Detach from the outcome, focus on the process.
You can do everything right on a deal and still lose it to budget cuts or internal politics. If your self-worth swings with every closed-won or closed-lost, you'll burn out. Focus on running a clean process and showing up every day. The numbers take care of themselves.

If you're a Product Manager looking to level up your impact, stop taking another framework course and learn SQL.

Here's why:

1. You stop waiting in the data queue.
When you rely on busy data analysts for every ad-hoc query, answering simple questions ("How many users dropped off at step 3 this week?") takes days. When you know basic SQL, you have answers in 10 minutes.

2. You build real intuition for your product.
Reading dashboards built by someone else only shows you aggregated metrics. Digging into the raw tables yourself allows you to spot edge cases, unexpected user behaviors, and hidden drop-offs that standard reports gloss over.

3. You earn instant credibility with engineering.
When you understand database schemas, relational joins, and query costs, your feature specs become sharper, more realistic, and much easier for engineers to estimate.

You don't need to be a DBA. Basic SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY, and JOIN statements will get you 80% of the value.

It's one of the highest-ROI technical skills a PM can learn.

A few years ago, I felt like I was working 10 hours a day but finishing every week wondering what I had actually accomplished. 

My calendar was full of 30-minute meetings, Slack was dinging every three minutes, and my brain felt constantly fragmented.

Then I read *Deep Work* by Cal Newport. It fundamentally changed how I view productivity and design my workday.

Three takeaways that transformed my routine:

1. Shallow work is addictive because it feels productive.
Clearing inboxes, responding quickly on Slack, and attending status meetings give you instant dopamine hits, but they rarely create durable value. Real progress comes from uninterrupted cognitive focus.

2. Multitasking is an illusion.
Every time you switch between writing a proposal and checking a notification, you leave "attention residue" behind. Your brain takes 15–20 minutes to get back to peak focus.

3. Schedule focus time like a client meeting.
I now block out two 90-minute "deep work" blocks on my calendar every week where Slack is snoozed, email is closed, and notifications are off. That's when the actual hard thinking happens.

In an economy where distraction is the default, the ability to focus deeply on hard problems is becoming a rare and valuable superpower.

Have you read it? What system helps you protect your focus?

Ten years ago this month, I put on scrubs for my first official shift as a registered nurse.

A decade in healthcare changes you in ways that are hard to describe to anyone outside the hospital walls.

I've held the hands of patients taking their last breaths. I've celebrated with families when cancer went into remission. I've worked 14-hour shifts on my feet without a bathroom break, cried in supply closets, and bonded with colleagues under pressures that forge friendships for life.

If nursing has taught me anything, it's this:
• Life is terrifyingly fragile. Health and time with people you love are the only things that truly matter.
• Kindness costs nothing, but to a terrified patient in a cold room, it changes everything.
• Healthcare workers give so much of their hearts every single day, often inside systems that don't support them enough.

To my fellow nurses and healthcare colleagues: thank you for showing up shift after shift. 

Here’s to 10 years of healing, learning, and caring.

As a recruiter who has interviewed over 1,500 candidates, here is the #1 mistake I see talented people make:

Focusing entirely on *what* they did, without explaining *why it mattered*.

Too many candidates answer behavioral questions like a checklist:
"I managed the email marketing campaign, set up automated drip sequences, and ran A/B tests on the subject lines."

That tells me your daily responsibilities, but it doesn't tell me your impact.

What outstanding candidates do instead:
"We noticed our onboarding churn was at 18%. I hypothesized that new users weren't activating key features in their first 48 hours. I rebuilt the email onboarding sequence with targeted feature prompts, which increased 30-day retention by 6% and drove an estimated $40k in ARR."

Context + Action + Business Result.

Companies don't just hire people to complete tasks. They hire people to solve business problems. 

Before your next interview, look at your resume bullets and ask yourself: "So what? What changed for the company because I did this?" That's your answer.

Cloud bills have a way of quietly spiraling out of control until someone in finance taps you on the shoulder.

Idle instances, unattached EBS volumes, oversized clusters, and egress fees—it's easy to waste 20–30% of your monthly cloud spend without realizing it.

We'll cover:
- Quick wins you can implement this week to eliminate immediate waste

- Setting up alerts and tagging governance so costs don't creep back up

No sales pitch, just practical engineering takeaways you can take straight back to your team.

Two years ago, I stood in front of a classroom of 30 high school students, wondering if it was too late to completely reinvent my career.

Today, I’m celebrating my first anniversary as a Product Designer.

When I first considered leaving teaching for UX design, I battled serious imposter syndrome. I didn't have a design degree, and I didn't know Figma. 

But as I transitioned, I realized that teaching was actually the best design training I could have asked for:
• Empathy: Understanding how 30 completely different learners process information is the exact same skill as understanding diverse user behaviors.
• Information Architecture: Structuring a curriculum isn't fundamentally different from mapping user flows and onboarding experiences.
• Collaboration & Feedback: When you spend years managing classrooms and parent conferences, handling stakeholder critiques and cross-functional feedback is second nature.

To anyone feeling "stuck" in their current field: your past experience isn't wasted time. It's your unique lens.

Skills like Figma and wireframing can be learned. Perspective and empathy are what make you great at the job. 🎨✨

#CareerChange #UXDesign #CareerTransition #ProductDesign #TeacherToTech

Early in your career, you grow by saying "yes" to everything.
Yes to every project.
Yes to every committee.
Yes to late-night emergency requests.

It proves you're eager, helpful, and dependable.

But as you advance, the skill that drives your growth completely flips. Your success stops being about what you take on, and starts being about what you protect yourself from.

Every time you say "yes" to something unimportant, you are implicitly saying "no" to:
- Deep focus on your primary high-impact goals
- Strategic thinking that moves your career forward
- Your evening, your sleep, and your mental health

Saying "no" doesn't mean being rude or uncooperative. It sounds like:
"I’d love to help, but if I take this on, it will delay [Priority Project X]. Which should we prioritize?"

Protecting your time isn't selfish. It's the only way to deliver exceptional work on the things that actually matter.

One year ago today, I quit my agency job and went full-time freelance as a designer.

The first year was exhilarating, terrifying, and deeply educational. 

Here are four honest lessons from year one:

1. Being great at design is only 30% of the job.
The other 70% is sales, client communication, scoping, contract negotiation, and bookkeeping. If you don't enjoy running a business, freelancing will burn you out quickly.

2. Scope creep isn't the client's fault; it's yours.
Every time a project ballooned out of control, it was because I didn't set clear boundaries and detailed deliverables in the contract upfront. Clear boundaries keep relationships healthy.

3. Feast or famine is real if you only market when you're slow.
When you're drowning in client work, the last thing you want to do is network or post updates. But if you stop pipeline building during busy months, you pay for it two months later. Always keep planting seeds.

4. Freedom is the best perk, but discipline is the price.
No boss checking in on you is amazing until you realize nobody is forcing you to sit at your desk either. Routine and boundaries are the only things that protect your freedom.

Year one in the books. To all my clients and fellow freelancers who cheered me on: thank you! Here's to year two.
